title: slow-brew-paper-caddy-owen-patel-2028
body:
Slow-brew reading caddy — brain-dump + first-pass synth of papers and ideas around long-context kv caches, eviction heuristics, and production-friendly fallbacks. Goal: collect surprising ideas and pragmatic experiments we can run on the Redwood stack without rewriting the runtime. No formal structure — this is a chew-and-notes doc.

Top-level takeaways (short):
- Many papers focus on improving model-level long-range attention but fewer give operational heuristics for KV cache management at inference serving scale.
- Eviction policy matters far more than people expect: sequence-aware heuristics (recency + semantic importance) beat pure LRU for multi-session, multi-user workloads.
- Tiny verification harnesses (synthetic TTL sessions + replay) reveal regressions in output quality quickly — build a lightweight CI for cache changes.

Papers skimmed in this pass (quick notes):
- "Compositional KV Cache Pruning" (arXiv 2803.01234) — idea: prune entries based on a learned salience predictor that takes prefix tokens + keys. Implementation note: predictor can run on CPU asynchronously and assign scores; we still need tight upper bound on pruning latency. Good fit for Dedicated where we have spare CPU cores.
- "TTL-based Session Windows" (conference short) — TTL heuristics per-customer: absolute time + activity-based reset. Pro: simple, deterministic; Con: underestimates semantic importance for infrequently referenced entities.
- "Semantic Sticky Tokens" — store small semantic fingerprints with KV entries to enable cluster-level deduplication; reduces total memory by 8-15% in their eval but needs a fast fingerprint compute. Could piggyback on embedding op.

My quick experiment sketches (how I'd try this on Redwood):
1) Synthetic session generator: create 10k synthetic sessions with mixes of long-running chat (500-2k tokens) and short bursts (10-50 tokens). Measure memory and average latency with varying eviction polices.
   - Metrics: median/95/99 latency, token cost, model output delta (BLEU/embedding-distance vs baseline).
   - Baselines: LRU, LFU, TTL=10m, learnt-salience (sim simulated scores).
2) Async salience scoring: implement a prototype where runtime emits candidate kv entries to sidecar scoring service (small Python worker). Sidecar returns priority and optional retention hint. Prototype should ensure scoring off the critical path — this is key.
3) Fallback correctness test harness: when an entry is pruned temporarily, how often does generation materially change? Build probes that run small prompt sets before and after pruning to measure semantic drift.

Open questions and heuristics to test:
- How to define "semantic importance" cheaply? Option: use low-dim embedding L2 distance between new tokens and stored keys. Cheap to compute if we already do embeddings.
- Eviction coordination across GPUs: should we move from per-GPU LRU to global budgeted eviction? Tradeoffs: global gives better memory utilization but requires cross-node signaling. Perhaps hybrid: soft local budgets with periodic rebalancing.
- Prefix caching vs chunked caching: store only chunked compressed KV frames for older prefixes. Compression introduces CPU cost — need a benchmark threshold (e.g., compress if entry idle > 30m).

Notes about rollout and safety:
- Any change to eviction should be feature-flagged per-customer. Start on Dedicated customers with lower SLA risk and opt-in for Hosted beta.
- Expose a per-tenant heuristic override in Console (TTL override, allowlist for "sticky" contexts).
- Add quick debugging surface: when a generation shifts after eviction change, log the nearest neighbor embedding distances and show the pruned keys (helps engineer triage).

Action items (next week):
- [ ] Build synthetic session generator (Owen) — aim for 10k sessions, paramizable.
- [ ] Prototype sidecar scoring service using an existing embedding model (Mira). CPU-bound proof-of-concept.
- [ ] Draft Eval plan for fallback correctness probes (Zoe) — include metric thresholds for rollout.
- [ ] Add a small Console toggle for per-tenant TTL overrides (product spike).

Quick notes-to-self about infra cost:
- Scoring sidecar will increase per-request tail only if mis-designed. Plan: emit events (not sync calls) and keep soft hints; critical path uses existing policies.
- Compression of cold entries looks promising but must be measured vs. added latency on cold reload. Potentially compress to int8 quantized frame.

Stray thoughts (coffee notes):
- Might be able to reuse the Optimize heuristic engine to suggest per-tenant TTLs based on observed session lifecycles (auto-tune).
- A "replay-and-verify" mode during rollout could mitigate quality regressions: new eviction policy runs in shadow and we compare outputs on a small sampling stream.

References / bookmarks for follow-up reads:
- arXiv:2803.01234 (Compositional KV Cache Pruning)
- internal PR: github.com/redwood-inference/kv-cache-experiments/pull/42 (old experiment harness)
- CONFLUENCE-REDWOOD-1234 — notes on previous TTL attempts

Questions for team sync:
1) Is there appetite to expose per-tenant cache control in the Console? (Product)
2) What are SRE concerns with cross-node eviction coordination? (SRE)
3) Could we get a small Dedicated customer to run an opt-in beta for the sidecar scoring idea? (Sales/Customer Success)

End. This is intentionally messy — use as seed for a proper RFC once we have some numbers from the synthetic generator.
